item.title: Bali’s fishing canoes are vanishing as tourism changes Indonesia’s coastline
item.description: The traditional boats with colourful carvings of the mythical elephant-fish on their prows represent centuries of maritime heritage.
item.content:encoded:
Five decades ago, Bali’s coastline was adorned with traditional fishing canoes with colourful carvings of mythical elephant-fish. Where did they go?

The disappearance of these canoes tells a much bigger story about how tourism, collecting and coastal change are reshaping Indonesia’s living maritime heritage – and why preserving these traditions matters.

The boats that once lined Bali’s beaches

Before Bali became one of the worlds’ most popular tourist destinations, fishing villages lined the beaches of Benoa, Nusa Dua and Sanur, along the island’s southern coast.

Generations of fishers built and sailed jukung pelasan – traditional timber double-outrigger sailing canoes with colourful carved gajah mina (elephant-fish) prows.

The gajah mina is a creature in Balinese Hindu tradition with the head of an elephant and the body of a fish. Symbolising unity and harmony between land and sea, it is said to protect crews during voyages and provide safe passage.

These were not just fishing boats; they were central to daily life in southern Bali.

The jukung were symbols of status and community identity. They embodied generations of craftsmanship, spiritual belief and maritime knowledge. They expressed the economic, social and spiritual life of Bali’s coastal communities, and reflected the enduring relationship between its people and the sea.

Today, however, only a handful remain.

item.title: Karnataka Congress MLA resigns after DK Shivakumar announces first Cabinet expansion
item.description: It was not possible to ‘accommodate everyone’, said the chief minister.
item.content:encoded:
Karnataka Congress MLA Yashwanthrayagouda Patil resigned from the Assembly on Monday, hours after the DK Shivakumar government announced its first expansion of the state Cabinet, The Indian Express reported.

Patil said that he had been “hurt” for being overlooked for a ministerial berth.

“I have been in politics for four decades,” the newspaper quoted Patil as saying. He added that he would decide whether he would quit the party or not.

Another Congress MLA Belur Gopalkrishna also said that he would resign from the Assembly as well as the chairperson of the Karnataka State Forest Industries Corporation.

“Only if you are children of chief ministers or ministers, will you have a chance [of becoming a minister]...,” The Indian Express quoted Gopalkrishna as saying.

Of the 20 MLAs inducted on Monday, 10 are first-time ministers, The Hindu reported.

Reacting to the developments, Shivakumar said that it was not possible to “accommodate everyone”.

“There are many MLAs,” The Indian Express quoted Shivakumar as saying. “...Earlier, I too missed out on a ministerial berth in the Siddaramaiah Cabinet. But didn’t I become a minister later?”

Shivakumar became the chief minister of Karnataka on June 3, replacing Siddaramaiah.

item.title: SC dismisses plea against clean chit to BJP’s Anurag Thakur, Parvesh Verma in hate speech case
item.description: The bench said that it had not found any grounds warranting reconsideration of its April decision.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court has dismissed a petition seeking review of its April decision, which held that no cognisable offence had been made out against Bharatiya Janata Party leaders Anurag Thakur and Parvesh Verma for alleged acts of hate speech in 2020, reported Bar and Bench on Monday.

At a rally in January 2020, Thakur was heard shouting “desh ke gaddaron ko” and the crowd responded with “goli maaro saalon ko”. The slogan meant “shoot the traitors”, with an expletive used for “traitors” being a reference to those protesting against the Citizenship Amendment Act.

In his speech, Verma had told an audience that the “lakhs of protestors” who had gathered at Delhi’s Shaheen Bagh would enter their homes to “rape their sisters and daughters and kill them”.

The speeches were made ahead of the Assembly elections in Delhi in 2020. Soon after, riots had broken out in North East Delhi in February that year, in which 53 persons died and hundreds were injured. The majority of victims were Muslim.

The April 29 decision by the Supreme Court came on a petition filed by Communist Party of India (Marxist) leader Brinda Karat against a Delhi High Court order that upheld a trial court’s refusal to direct the registration of a case against the BJP leaders.

item.title: India’s rhetoric on a two-state solution in Palestine is at odds with Israel’s geographical reorderi
item.description: This language describes a country that no longer exists in any contiguous form while Israel expands its grip on the region.
item.content:encoded:
On July 7, Narendra Modi stood beside Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto in Jakarta and declared that India supports “a two-state solution and the pursuit of lasting peace” in Palestine. Modi was repeating a line that Indian prime ministers have recited for decades. It is a comfortable formulation that costs New Delhi nothing and offends no one.

A week later, Indian officials at the Palestine Donor Group meetings in Brussels reiterated the commitment, welcoming diplomatic avenues towards Palestinian statehood and UN membership.

But this language now describes a country that no longer exists in any coherent, contiguous form, and every week that passes widens the gap between rhetoric and reality.

On July 14, just a week after Modi’s Jakarta remarks, Israel’s security cabinet approved a budget of $434 million to establish 34 new settlements in the occupied West Bank. This is the latest move in a wider settlement project, the scale of which makes the two-state framework difficult to sustain in its classical sense.

Israel’s settler expansion has drawn criticism abroad, but the same chasm between word and deed is visible closer to home. India has kept up its rhetorical support for Palestinian statehood even as it deepens its own ties with Israel.

item.title: Lucknow: Six kanwariyas allegedly attack school van, smash windscreen
item.description: The students in the vehicle were not injured, the police said.
item.content:encoded:
Six kanwariyas on three motorcycles allegedly attacked a school van in Uttar Pradesh’s Lucknow on Monday after a minor accident, The Indian Express reported. No children were injured.

During the Kanwar Yatra, devotees, called kanwariyas, walk hundreds of kilometres to collect water from the Ganga near Haridwar and carry it back to their home states to offer at temples.

The incident on Monday took place at Charak Crossing in the Chowk area while the van was on its way to drop students at school. One of the motorcycles hit the rear of the vehicle after the van driver applied the brakes, which led to an argument.

The dispute prompted some of the kanwariyas to allegedly damage the van’s rear windshield and side mirror, before they fled.

item.title: New fiction: A woman grapples with motherhood during the Covid-19 pandemic
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Grief Burns Like Fever’, by Minakshi Thakur.
item.content:encoded:
We are bunkered down in the house, no contact with the world outside. My husband watches television all day. The news laps against my ears like waves at high tide. I constantly find myself in the kitchen – cooking, cleaning, doing the dishes, washing vegetables, chopping, cooking, cleaning. Rinse and repeat. The skin on my hands is eroding; bits get washed away under the tap and fall into the drain, reaching god knows where. Between chores, I remember to pop my pills. I try to be regular and sometimes even set alarms on my phone. But when the alarms go off, I forget why I set them. My husband has taught me to write the purpose against the alarm, but it’s too much of a bother. In fact, to tell you the truth – and please don’t share this with anyone, for they will find it ludicrous – I am mortally scared of phones. item.title: Raj Thackeray alleges Rs 18 crore stolen from Mumbai’s Siddhivinayak temple every year
item.description: The Maharashtra Navnirman Sena chief claimed that Rs 1,400 crore had been ‘stolen’ from the Ram temple in Ayodhya.
item.content:encoded:
Maharashtra Navnirman Sena chief Raj Thackeray on Sunday alleged that donations worth Rs 18 crore had been embezzled from the Siddhivinayak temple in Mumbai every year.

He also claimed that Rs 1,400 crore had been “stolen” from the Ram temple in Ayodhya.

The remarks came amid a row over the alleged embezzlement of donations at the Ram temple in Uttar Pradesh.

On Sunday, citing a letter purportedly written by eight temple trustees to Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde, Thackeray claimed that employees at Siddhivinayak temple had siphoned off donations from collection boxes.

He also claimed that the temple’s weekly donations were below Rs 50 lakh before the alleged theft came to light, but increased to about Rs 1.5 crore after those allegedly involved were caught.

Sada Sarvankar, chairperson of the Siddhivinayak Temple Trust and a leader of the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena, said that nine temple employees had been arrested in connection with the alleged theft, PTI reported.

“We have filed cases wherever required,” the news agency quoted Sarvankar as saying.

item.title: Kerala: 15 killed in rain-related incidents, seven missing
item.description: The state government will provide Rs 10,000 in funeral expenses to the families of those who died, said Chief Minister VD Satheesan.
item.content:encoded:
The toll in rain-related incidents in Kerala has risen to 15, PTI quoted Chief Minister VD Satheesan as saying on Monday.

While he did not specify the period in which the deaths took place, the state has been receiving heavy and incessant rainfall since Friday, triggering flash floods and landslides.

Satheesan said on Monday that seven persons were missing amid the rains. Of these, two persons each were missing from Kollam and Kannur, and one each in Malappuram, Idukki and Muvattupuzha.

Malappuram had reported four deaths, while three persons died in Kottayam district. Two deaths each were reported in Ernakulam and Kollam, and one person each died in Idukki, Muvattupuzha and Kannur.

The chief minister announced that the state government will provide Rs 10,000 in funeral expenses to the families of those who died. Persons returning home from relief camps would receive Rs 10,000 as an immediate measure.

Additionally, an ex gratia of Rs 8 lakh was announced for the families of those who died. A compensation of Rs 12 lakh will be given to those who lost their homes and land due to landslides. Rs 6 lakh will be provided for families to rebuild their homes, said Satheesan.

item.title: Youth protests: Supreme Court clarifies states can withdraw FIRs against demonstrators
item.description: The statement came after the Centre submitted that it was ‘serious’ about its assurance that no coercive action will be taken against student protesters.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Monday clarified that states can withdraw first information reports filed against youth protesters wherever permissible, in accordance with the law, Live Law reported.

The clarification came in response to concerns raised by petitioners that the court’s July 28 order, which allowed states to continue investigations into the FIRs, could hinder the withdrawal of cases. They argued that closing the FIRs was part of the Union government’s promise to leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party political campaign to end the protests.

It also came after the Union government submitted that it was “serious” about its assurance that amnesty would be granted to students who had participated in demonstrations, The Hindu reported.

In its July 28 order, the Supreme Court had directed that minors who had been detained should be released and no coercive action should be taken against protesting students as long as they did not have any “criminal antecedents”.

On Monday, the bench also clarified that the term “criminal antecedents” in the order referred only to “grave and heinous offences”.

The Cockroach Janta Party campaign on Monday said that following the Supreme Court’s clarification it expects all states with Bharatiya Janata Party governments “to immediately honour the assurances given on 25 July to the young of this country”.

item.description: Three accounts of the party have been blocked by the central agency in connection with alleged financial irregularities.

The Supreme Court on Monday asked the Enforcement Directorate whether a limited amount of funds from the Trinamool Congress’ frozen bank accounts could be released to a court-appointed administrator for the party to meet its daily expenses, Bar and Bench reported.

The bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale was hearing a plea by the Mamata Banerjee-led faction of the TMC challenging the Calcutta High Court order.

The High Court had on July 20 refused to allow the TMC to operate three bank accounts frozen by the ED. The party had approached the High Court challenging the probe agency’s action under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.

The case pertains to alleged financial irregularities, unlawful collection of money and routing of suspected funds through certain bank accounts of the TMC.

On June 19, the Kolkata Police froze debit operations on the accounts, a day after rebel TMC MLA Biswanath Das filed a complaint alleging that funds had been misused. The party has been grappling with factionalism after its loss in the West Bengal Assembly elections in May.

item.title: Bangladesh: Hindu monk Chinmoy Krishna Das gets bail, will remain in jail in four other cases
item.description: The court granted him relief in two cases pertaining to attempted murder and obstructing police officers from discharging their duties.
item.content:encoded:
Bangladesh’s High Court on Sunday granted bail to Hindu religious leader Chinmoy Krishna Das in two cases, The Daily Star reported. However, he will not be released from prison as he is accused in four other cases.

The monk, who was formerly associated with the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, has been in jail since November 25, 2024. He was arrested for allegedly disrespecting Bangladesh’s national flag during a rally on October 25 that year in Chittagong.

He is the spokesperson of the Sammilito Sanatani Jagaron Jote, an organisation that advocates for the rights of Hindus and other minorities in Bangladesh.

The two cases in which he was granted bail on Sunday pertain to attempted murder and obstructing police officers from discharging their duties.

The murder case is about the death of a public prosecutor during clashes that broke out on November 26, 2024, between Das’ supporters and lawyers near the Chattogram Court, when his bail petition was rejected.

The police alleged that the Hindu leader’s followers blocked the prison van in which he was travelling, prompting the clash during which a lawyer, Saiful Islam Alif, was hacked to death.

And one of the key contributors in this journey of grit and strength was his competence in sports.

item.title: BJP weaponising NSA to silence dissent, says Congress on Assam activist Pranab Doley’s detention
item.description: ‘Similar attempts have been witnessed in Uttar Pradesh, where the Act was invoked against labour activists protesting in Noida,’ said Jairam Ramesh.
item.content:encoded:
The Assam government invoking the National Security Act against activist Pranab Doley was part of a “growing pattern” of the Bharatiya Janata Party “weaponising extraordinary laws to silence dissent”, alleged the Congress on Monday.

The Act allows for long periods of detention without trial up to a year.

Doley was arrested on July 12, days after he took part in a protest against a hotel project at Ingle Pathar, a village adjoining the Kaziranga National Park.

The police had alleged that he “unlawfully trespassed into the site of the Tea Tribes Museum and thereafter trespassed into the nearby ATDC [Assam Tourism Development Corporation] Hyatt project at Ingle Pathar with deadly weapons” during the protest.

On July 29, a sessions court in Golaghat granted bail to Doley, stating that the investigating officer had already recorded the statements of key witnesses and that there was no possibility of the accused concealing or tampering with evidence.

A day later, the BJP government in Assam detained him under the National Security Act, alleging that Doley had carried out “suspicious foreign transactions from doubtful sources” in violation of the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act.

This meant that he was not released from jail, despite the bail order.

Both Houses of Parliament were adjourned till 2 pm after they reconvened on Monday amid a ruckus following demands by the Opposition that Union Home Minister Amit Shah be present for a discussion on the crackdown on youth protesters on July 20.

The proceedings in the Lok Sabha were paused for an hour, barely four minutes after the House convened at 11 am. At 12.09 pm, the Lower House was adjourned again till 2 pm. The Rajya Sabha was adjourned at 11.20 am.

The Opposition parties have been demanding that Shah make a statement in Parliament about the use of force by security personnel against student protesters in Delhi on July 20. The police in the national capital and the central armed police forces report to the Union Ministry of Home Affairs.

item.title: Special judge in Delhi fast-track court for paper leak cases transferred
item.description: The court was among those instituted on July 23 amid youth protests over alleged irregularities in the conduct of competitive exams.
item.content:encoded:
A judicial officer appointed as the special judge of a fast-track court to hear paper leak cases was transferred on Saturday as part of a reshuffle in the Delhi Higher Judicial Service.

The transfer came just nine days after the Delhi High Court designated Judge Anu Grover Baliga to head the special fast-track court at the Rouse Avenue Court Complex to try offences under the 2024 Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Act.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi had announced the setting up of fast-track courts on July 23 amid nationwide youth protests over alleged irregularities in conducting competitive examinations.

Following the transfer, the paper leak cases, including those related to the 2026 undergraduate National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test, will be heard by Special Judge Ajay Gupta.

Gupta had been hearing the NEET case before the fast-track court was constituted, The Indian Express reported.

The first proceedings in the fast-track court were deferred on July 27 after no counsel represented the Central Bureau of Investigation. The absence of the prosecutor was highlighted when the judge was to hear the bail applications of two men accused in the case.

Baliga, along with Vikas Dhull, Prashant Sharma, Amit Bansal, Kiran Bansal and Pulastya, has been appointed as special National Investigation Agency judge to hear cases related to terrorism.

BJP’s Samrat Choudhary replaced Janata Dal (United) chief Nitish Kumar as chief minister in April.

item.title: Start the week with a film: ‘In The Heat of the Night’ follows a murder and one of the oldest crimes
item.description: Norman Jewison’s Oscar-winning drama stars Sidney Poitier and Rod Steiger.
item.content:encoded:
Virgil Tibbs is arrested for the murder of the wealthy industrialist Philip Colbert. In the eyes of the local cops, Virgil has every reason to be a suspect: he has a wallet full of money; he’s leaving town; he’s Black.

The last factor is the most important in this small American town seething with racism. When Virgil (Sidney Poitier) reveals that he too is a police detective from Philadelphia, who was passing through town, the local police chief Bill (Rod Steiger) is gobsmacked.

Vigril wants to leave on the next available train, but his investigative skills are superior to those of Bill and his posse. Bill takes Virgil’s help to solve the murder, hating nearly every minute of it and not holding back with his feelings either.

Ceuta, an autonomous city, sits on Morocco’s northern coast. The Spanish government has said almost all of the migrants have since returned to Morocco, and at least 57 have died.

item.title: How Shakespeare’s ‘The Tempest’ can help readers understand the hidden costs of AI
item.description: The play offers a useful means of understanding how power operates through hidden infrastructures.
item.content:encoded:
In the 400 years since his death, William Shakespeare’s work has been used as a lens through which to interpret countless developments he could never have anticipated – from modern psychology and political theory to colonialism and climate change. His writing possesses an uncanny ability to illuminate nearly every facet of the human condition.

Yet, as a decolonial scholar and an AI researcher, we believe that Shakespeare’s plays are now beginning to illuminate something beyond that as well – the emergent forms of artificial intelligence that increasingly shape and challenge our understanding of what it means to think, act and be.

AI tools have rapidly become part of many people’s everyday lives. Yet relatively few probably consider the physical infrastructure that makes these systems possible. Each prompt we send is processed in distant data centres: vast facilities that generate responses by predicting the most likely sequence of words based on patterns learned from enormous datasets.

This dynamic of distant, unseen control recalls Shakespeare’s The Tempest, a play that offers a useful means of understanding how power operates through hidden infrastructures.

In South Mumbai’s Mandvi Koliwada sits a terracotta-colored building bearing the name Janabai and Madhavrao Rokade Municipal School.

As is the case with public buildings in many Indian cities, the names of the personalities that adorn them are often unfamiliar. Some of them are linked to relatively recent politicians and cultural figures. A few of them have a deeper historical connection. The Rokade municipal school falls in the second category.

The school was established in 1879, making it one of Mumbai’s earliest modern schools. It was started by Madhavrao Rokade.

item.title: Protests were about accountability. For that, India’s Gen Z will have to keep asking hard questions
item.description: The government’s concessions have not disrupted the arrangement that produced these grievances in the first place.
item.content:encoded:
In a little over a month, the Cockroach Janata Party-led student movement that began as a joke held one of the world’s most immovable governments to a single demand and won. When Dharmendra Pradhan resigned as education minister on July 25, the students who had occupied Jantar Mantar wept and embraced. Abhijeet Dipke, who founded the movement, fell to his knees.

Since coming to power in 2014, the Bharatiya Janata Party government has rarely bowed to public pressure, and almost never to the young. The repeal of the farm laws in 2021 is remembered because such retreats are so uncommon.

item.title: How lab-grown diamonds have changed the game
item.description: The saying goes that ‘diamonds are forever’. But what if the market for them isn’t?
item.content:encoded:
You’ve probably heard the saying “a diamond is forever”. What if the market for them – with its hefty price tags – isn’t?

Back in March, Rio Tinto ended production at its Diavik diamond mine in Canada after 23 years. Earlier this month, diamond mining company De Beers announced a two-year production pause at the company’s flagship Venetia mine in South Africa.

De Beers is majority-owned by global mining giant Anglo American. According to a Bloomberg report this week, Anglo is now in talks to sell its 85% stake for about US$1 billion – a tiny fraction of the US$18 billion it was valued at when taken private in 2001.

So, what’s going on? The industry certainly hasn’t run out of diamonds to mine. But current prices and costs have made continued production of natural diamonds harder to justify.

Over the past couple of decades, lab-grown diamonds have changed the game. Consumers are also reconsidering what makes a diamond valuable – and what responsible consumption means.

In the mid-nineteenth century, aluminium was treated as a luxury material and its value exceeded that of gold. While it was abundant in the Earth’s crust, it was difficult and expensive to isolate and refine.

item.title: Who was Homer, author of the ‘Odyssey’?
item.description: When the ‘Odyssey’ first began to circulate in ancient Greece, no one knew its author. The song seems to have created the singer, not the other way around.
item.content:encoded:
Who wrote the Odyssey?

Homer, obviously: that is what we’ve been told since the late 6th century BCE, when ancient Greeks started crediting the Odyssey to a blind bard from the rocky isle of Chios.

But this “Homer” appeared at least a century later than the poem itself. When the Odyssey first began to circulate in ancient Greece, no one knew its author. The song seems to have created the singer, not the other way around.

How can you have a poem without a poet? Two American researchers, Milman Parry and Albert Lord, came across a possible answer.

In the 1930s, Parry and Lord travelled to the Balkans to study still-living traditions of epic poetry. In Yugoslavia and Albania, they found bards who sang of heroes from long ago. These singers did not recite from a book. Most of them couldn’t read or write at all. Instead, they improvised their epics as they sang. They knew the story by heart, but told it in different words with each performance.

Balkan bards achieved this by relying on a stock of formulaic scenes, lines and phrases, which they combined on the spot. The formulae were passed down from teacher to student, so that all singers tended to sound alike.

This telltale style is just what we find in Homeric poetry....

item.title: Can fuel-reliant South Asia survive the next global conflict?
item.description: The oil-importing countries of Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka must invest in building energy security.

Amid signs that the US and Iran have paused their latest round of hostilities, it is time to examine the economies that the conflict effectively brought to a standstill this year.

In March 2026, when the exchange of threats and missiles choked the Strait of Hormuz, the bill landed on the doors of Dhaka, Islamabad and Colombo long before it reached Washington or Brussels.

The moment revealed itself less as a geopolitical crisis and more as unending queues for fuel in South Asia, with restaurants shuttered and households plunged into darkness by relentless load shedding.

Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka – three countries with virtually no domestic oil reserves and no meaningful influence over global commodity prices – absorbed energy shocks for a war they did not cause. That is the nature of fossil-fuel dependence in South Asia, and it is not new. The 2008 oil price bubble and subsequent spike. The 2022 Russia‑Ukraine war in which Russia limited supplies and caused gas price shocks. These are other chapters in the same structural story.

The title of Sutapa Banerjee’s edited volume, The Business of Business Is (Not) Just Business, underlines something that few would argue against. The era when businesses could legitimately argue that the only responsibility they have is to their shareholders is behind us. The role of business is widely acknowledged to encompass a much larger range of stakeholders. Businesses are not exempt from society; they play an active role in shaping it not just in economic terms but also culturally. Employment, migration, gender, environment, aspirations, access to opportunity, public discourse and the very idea of progress are all shaped in some way or the other by business.

item.title: August Indian nonfiction: Six new titles that take a closer look at 79 years of independence
item.description: A journalist’s report from India’s Maoist hotbed, a genius mathematician’s biography, an examination of India’s social policy, and more.
item.content:encoded:
All information sourced from publishers.

DD Kosambi: One Life Many Worlds, Ram Ramaswamy

Historian. Mathematician. Marxist. Polymath. DD Kosambi defied labels. The range and intellectual heft of his scholarship was truly astounding, with fundamental contributions in differential geometry and analyses in mathematics, the Kosambi distance in genetics, a statistical analysis of ancient coin hoards, a radical reinterpretation of Indian history and stellar compilations of the poetry of Vidyakara and Bhartrhari-all this in addition to a firm commitment to world peace and environmental activism.

Yet, for a man who contributed so much to the Indian intellectual tradition, he remains largely unknown. Sixty years after his passing, there is scant recognition of his talents-he is quoted more often than he is read and praised more often than he is analysed.

Ram Ramaswamy’s biography of Kosambi seeks to correct this lapse. Set against the backdrop of fascinating social, political, scientific and historiographical transformation in the subcontinent, and drawing from letters, journal entries, family accounts and unprecedented archival material, DD Kosambi: One Life, Many Worlds reveals a rare incandescent genius and a fearless independent spirit with boundless curiosity-whose relevance in the fields of pedagogy, research and invention can be seen even today.

item.title: The story of Kerala’s first female writer-composer who transcended her time
item.description: Kuttykunju Thangkachi broke new ground in music, theatre and literature at a time when women’s creativity was expected to remain private.
item.content:encoded:
A gaunt elderly woman, her face sombre and framed by wispy grey hair left loose over her shoulders, gazes out in the side-profile. She wears the unmistakable symbols of an upper caste elite woman from 19th-century Kerala: the mundu mulakacha wrap tied across her chest, layers of gold around her neck, and a yawning ear piercing that signals a lifetime of wearing heavy gold earrings. Yet to dismiss Kuttykunju Thangkachi as merely a privileged noblewoman would be a profound mistake.

The tumultuous 84 years of her life, which ended in 1904, were packed with triumphs virtually unheard of for women of her era. She was the earliest female dramatist in Malayalam with her play Ajnatavasam, the first woman to write attakathas, or librettos, for Kathakali, and a prolific creator across Kerala’s indigenous musical forms, including kummi, thiruvathira pattu, kurathipattu and thullal. Crucially, she was the first female Carnatic composer from Kerala at a time when only men were accorded the elevated title of vaggeyakara (writer-composer).

item.title: In Nicaragua, President Ortega bans elections – a new page in the authoritarian playbook
item.description: This shows a growing brazenness among autocratic regimes and a declining concern for international legitimacy.
item.content:encoded:
Since being elected for a second term as Nicaraguan president in 2006, Daniel Ortega – the former Sandinista freedom fighter-turned-authoritarian leader – has extended his term of office several times. But last week he announced a new strategy for holding on to power.

He declared that there will no longer be elections in the Central American country. Making a speech to commemorate the anniversary of the 1979 revolution that toppled the Somoza dictatorship which had ruled Nicaragua since 1937, he said: “The days when parties backed by the Yankees and the Somocistas would return to power are over – never again.” The legal changes are already moving through the country’s legislature.

Nicaragua’s elections have long been rigged and repressive. But this marks a new scale of authoritarian rule. The elimination of elections is a rare and extreme case, even in today’s landscape of authoritarian regimes. So this reflects a worrying trend of brazenness on the part of Nicaragua’s president.

Spin dictators

Most modern autocrats are what researchers call “spin dictators”. They invest in a democratic disguise and the careful curation of a public image fostered by propaganda and misinformation. Elections play a central role in this playbook.

item.title: Deluge with monsoon deficit is India’s new climate normal
item.description: Climate change is no longer about more or less rainfall but is redistributing water in increasingly unpredictable ways.
item.content:encoded:
In the first week of July, in Mumbai’s Mankhurd, torrential monsoon rains triggered a building collapse that buried five children beneath the debris, transforming one of the city’s wettest July days in half a century into a humanitarian tragedy. Streets disappeared beneath floodwaters, transport networks ground to a halt, and emergency services struggled to reach stranded residents.

Thousands of kilometres away, London faced an entirely different manifestation of the same crisis. During the June 2026 heatwave, temperatures exceeded 36 degrees celsius, commuters fainted inside sweltering Underground trains, and climate activists covered Tube stations with stickers reading, “Heatwave, sponsored by Shell”, highlighting the perceived role of fossil fuels in intensifying global warming.

These events unfolded in vastly different economic and geographic settings. Yet they reflected a common reality: climate change no longer distinguishes between developed and developing nations. Whether through floods, heatwaves, landslides or dust storms, extreme weather is increasingly becoming the defining challenge of the twenty-first century.

The scientific evidence underpinning this reality has become overwhelming. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) reported in 2023 that the global mean near-surface temperature in 2023 was 1.45 ± 0.12 degrees celsius above the pre-industrial average, bringing the world dangerously close to the 1.5 degrees celsius threshold established under the Paris Agreement.

item.title: E20 petrol can reduce fuel efficiency by 2% to 6% in some vehicles, Nitin Gadkari tells Parliament

Citing studies by government agencies and automobile manufacturers, Union Road Transport Minister Nitin Gadkari said that the reduction in fuel efficiency was “influenced by several factors, including driving conditions, driving habits and vehicle maintenance”.

Gadkari added that tests on engine durability, drivability, startability, corrosion resistance and material compatibility had confirmed that E20 fuel was safe for use under prescribed standards.

item.description: Fewer children are dialling Childline for help in many states. Activists and staff say there is a sharp decline in the quality of assistance provided.

Usually, within 60 minutes of such a call, members of a local non-governmental organisation would have reached the spot.

But the call centre transferred the matter to the district child protection unit in Dhule. Instead of visiting the spot, an official contacted the organisation that had made the call, the Saptshrungi Bahuuddeshiya Mahila Sanstha, and asked it to inform the labour department. “He said this is not in their jurisdiction,” said a social worker from the Sanstha who did not want to be identified.

We go looking for the birds that have come from afar for the berries. The cold January dawn breaks along a dusty, smoky horizon in orange-red, paling to light blue. A factory belches smoke into the skies over the open landscape we drive through, here in the district of Kutch in northern Gujarat. We pass fields of castor, dry plants along dry furrows, clumps of the ubiquitous American mesquite, wires criss-crossing between large electric pylons, one carrying a perched Long-legged Buzzard morosely scanning the miles of field and fallow from horizon to horizon. item.title: Review: ‘The Legend of Karna’ imagines the Mahabharata warrior as a rugged disruptor

Ahead of a new film about the Ramayana comes an animated web series based on Karna from the Mahabharata. The Legend of Karna, out on Sony LIV, focuses on one of the Mahabharata’s most fascinating characters.

The first of the Pandava brothers, who is denied his inheritance because of his illegitimate birth and adoption by a low-caste charioteer, Karna has inspired close study. Yuganta, Irawati Karve’s magisterial analysis of the Mahabharata, devotes a chapter to Karna, who is perennially dogged by the question “Who am I?”

“He struggled all his life to gain what he thought was his rightful status and his bitterness lay in not having got it,” writes Karve.

Contemporary screen versions of the Mahabharata (Shyam Benegal’s Kalyug, Mani Ratnam’s Thalapathi) also emphasise Karna’s frustration and sorrow over his unjust treatment.

item.title: Why the BJP is struggling to crack Gen Z’s reel-driven algorithm
item.description: Instagram’s short-form video content, preferred by young Indians, is vastly different from the text-first social media that the BJP has dominated until now.
item.content:encoded:
Late on the night of July 23, Prime Minister Narendra Modi appeared on Instagram in an unusual selfie-video. His post went viral soon after – but for all the wrong reasons.

The video was aimed at addressing the growing anger among protesting young Indians, led by the fledgling Cockroach Janata Party movement, demanding the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over examination glitches and paper leaks.

Modi’s video was an attempt to reach out to students and young Indians on Instagram, a platform they have used to organise the protests. However, the video exemplified a complete algorithmic and cultural disconnect with how Gen Z communicates.

The prime minister’s upload violated almost every aesthetic rule of short-form content: it lacked an engaging visual hook, featured unusually slow speech and used an awkwardly-framed front-camera angle.

item.title: ‘What We Leave We Carry’: A ‘collective memoir’ of Britain sees migration as a reflective process
item.description: The book follows three or more generations of immigrants to understand what it means to be British today.

This is the right time for them to read Colin Grant’s What We Leave We Carry, a collective memoir of Britain that many rarely experience. It opens out a new map of the globe by compiling interviews with writers, thinkers, artists, engineers, and a diverse workforce about what makes Britain today what it is.

Listening to neighbours

This is how Grant presents the quest of the book: “This is an oral history of overlooked and marginalised individuals. It’s a chance to listen to neighbours, voices often drowned out by the shrill anti-immigrant rhetoric that is afforded too much space in our culture”.

The book follows three or more generations of immigrants to understand what it means to be British today. Migration is mapped across emotive, physical, and intellectual geographies. item.title: Three reasons why India’s household savings are falling despite a huge working-age population
item.description: Families are borrowing money for consumption, a sign of poor-quality, low-paying jobs while instruments to create savings are inadequate.
item.content:encoded:
India’s demographic dividend of a large, youthful workforce is being unsettled by a troubled trend: even as the share of working-age Indians climbs to record highs, household savings have fallen to their lowest level in nearly two decades.

This puzzle strikes at the heart of an influential economic theory.

In 1985, Franco Modigliani won the Nobel Prize for his life-cycle hypothesis of household savings. People spread out their consumption across a lifetime: borrowing when young, saving hard through their prime working years and drawing down those savings in retirement.

On a population scale, Modigliani’s theory implies that a country’s saving rate depends less on its wealth and more on how its people are distributed across the life cycle.

A nation with a bulge of prime-age workers should save a lot. Economists Ronald Lee and Andrew Mason later sharpened this insight into what they called the “second demographic dividend”.

The first dividend – the one India routinely celebrates – is the mechanical boost to output per person that comes from a rising share of working-age people. The second is subtler and, crucially, not guaranteed. It materialises only where pensions, formal financial systems and functioning labour markets allow the instinct to save for later life to translate into real, investable wealth.

item.content:encoded:
The Lok Sabha on Thursday passed a bill criminalising insults to the national song, Vande Mataram, a day after the Rajya Sabha cleared the legislation.

The bill will now be sent for presidential assent, after which it will become law.

The 2026 Prevention of Insults to National Honour Amendment Bill was passed in the Lok Sabha through a voice vote amid protests by Opposition MPs demanding a discussion on police action against youth protesters last week.

The protests were held against the alleged mismanagement in conducting competitive exams.

The bill seeks to provide Vande Mataram with the same statutory protection as the national anthem, Jana Gana Mana. It states that intentionally preventing the singing of the national song, or disrupting an assembly singing it can be punished with imprisonment of up to three years, a fine or both.

At present, the 1971 Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act provides that insulting the national anthem, Jana Gana Mana, the national flag or the Constitution is punishable with up to three years’ imprisonment, a fine or both.
